item.title: Ukraine: From reactive response to a culture of care [EN/UK]
item.description:
Country: Ukraine
Source: Prosper Global

Please refer to the attached files.

Institutionalizing Duty of Care for local partners in Ukraine

Local organizations deliver a large share of the humanitarian response in Ukraine, often closest to the front line and with the fewest protections. This report documents how Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps) in Ukraine moved from ad hoc, reactive support to an institutionalized Duty of Care Minimum Package for its local partners between 2022 and 2025. It sets out the nine options available to partners, how the package was embedded into partnership systems, what partners prioritized and which gaps remain. Key takeaway is that Duty of Care for partners works best when it is non-negotiable as a standard, yet flexible, risk-based and partner-led in its application.

Why Duty of Care matters

Humanitarian work in Ukraine is carried out under persistent threat. Aid workers and volunteers operate within range of artillery, missiles and drones. Offices and homes are damaged in attacks on cities far from the front line, and repeated strikes on energy infrastructure leave teams without power, heating and connectivity for hours or days. Constant air-raid alerts add a layer of cumulative stress that rarely disappears.

Local civil society organizations carry a disproportionate share of this risk. They are often the first to reach affected communities and the last to leave, yet they typically work with small teams, mixed employment arrangements and limited access to insurance, security expertise or psychosocial support. Shifting leadership to local actors without ensuring their protection transfers risk rather than power.

Prosper Global works in Ukraine primarily through partnerships, collaborating with around 35 local partners across humanitarian response, economic recovery, agriculture and energy resilience. A partner organization is not an aid-delivery channel but a community of professionals whose safety and well-being are integral to the success of the humanitarian mission.

item.title: IOM Yemen Dispatch October 2026
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian crisis worsened in October with the expanding ground offensives, intensifying cross-border air strikes, and severe strains on already fragile structures for essential services such as healthcare. Ansar Allah (AA) forces sustained their multi-axis offensives across southwestern fronts, continuing heavy assaults on the key frontlines in Taiz while launching multiple strikes at strategic structures including the Presidential Palace and International Airport in Aden. This led to large-scale movements, driving the cumulative number of newly displaced individuals to over 300,000 since June. Taiz became the main frontline and humanitarian concern when AA forces captured Al-Turbah and AsSafiyah, cutting the main Taiz–Aden Road and effectively encircling Taiz City. Key commercial and humanitarian transport corridors remained blocked or compromised, with severe access restrictions critically isolating the population in Taiz. AA forces expanded long-range ballistic missile and drone strikes against the International Airports, oil infrastructures, and military installations across Saudi Arabia, and Saudi-led coalition forces alongside the Government of Yemen (GoY) also intensified air strikes against key AA positions in Yemen. As of 27 October, OHCHR had documented 263 civilian casualties, including 67 people killed. Children accounted for 97 of the casualties and about half of those killed. With the surge in conflict casualties, major referral hospitals across Taiz, Lahj, Marib, and Hadramawt faced severe shortages of basic medical supplies, fuel, and medical oxygen, and were forced to suspend routine and elective care to prioritize trauma operations. The health emergency was compounded by damaged water treatment systems and overcrowded, unsanitary conditions in displacement sites across the top concentrated governorates such as Lahj, Abyan, Taiz, and Aden. Food security exacerbated as staple commodities and fuel prices increased steeply with the continuing supply chain blockades and worsening access situation. Depleted humanitarian stockpiles and severe underfunding raise concerns of acute malnutrition cases increasing, as estimated 5.4 million people in GoY-controlled areas are expected to be in IPC Phase 3 or worse food insecurity in the final quarter of the year. Both GoY and AA raised fuel prices in their respective areas of control in the last week of October, with official price of gasoline ranging between YR 570 per liter (AA-controlled area, 20% increase since midSeptember), YR 1,700 per liter (GoY-controlled area), and over YR 2,500 per liter in Taiz. The citizens are forced to purchase fuel in the black market, where petrol prices skyrocketed to over YR 150,000 for a 20-liter can, as most gas stations have shut down. Water production in Taiz city has fallen by about half due to the critical shortage of fuel.

item.title: IOM Yemen Dispatch Situation Overview September 2026
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian situation worsened significantly throughout September, driven by the continued spread of ground fighting following August’s violent escalations. Ground hostilities expanded rapidly across southwestern fronts, with Ansar Allah (AA) forces intensifying offensives in Ta’iz and Lahj as they attempted to consolidate gains on the West Coast by securing the overlooking mountains. The fighting triggered a massive surge in displacement, forcing over 160,140 individuals to flee their homes, particularly from the Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, and Al Ma’afer districts in Ta’iz. Vital supply lines, including the crucial road linking Mokha to Ta’iz City, were severely disrupted and cut off, stranding communities and impacting humanitarian access. The AA forces claimed to have targeted several sites in Riyadh and the Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Saudi Red Sea port, with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia requested air defenses for critical facilities from Egypt, France, Pakistan, and the UK. French President Emmanuel Macron said France would send military assets to help protect Yanbu following the attack, as the concerns over maritime security and global oil prices grew. Saudi Arabia also reportedly urged the Government of Yemen (GoY) to call for a general mobilization, which was announced in a speech marking the anniversary of the September 26 Revolution. On the other side, in a move to capitalize on its capture of the Bab al-Mandeb and the West Coast, the AA-affiliated Red Sea Ports and Tax Customs Authorities announced reductions in vessel and container fees and port taxes, effective 1 October. The sharp escalation in violence severely strained Yemen’s already compromised health infrastructure, with hospitals in Ta’iz, Ma’rib, and Hadramaut overwhelmed by casualties. Major health centers were forced to suspend non-emergency care—such as maternity and obstetrics services—to reallocate scarce beds and medical personnel toward trauma management. The cholera epidemic maintained a strong hold across southern and western governorates, with transmission exacerbated by population displacement and damaged water and sanitation infrastructure. Abyan and Lahj continued to report the highest concentration of suspected cases, while newly displaced clusters in Ta’iz and Aden saw rising incidence rates. According to the IPC, nearly five million people faced crisis levels of hunger or worse in government-controlled areas between March and May, including 1.4 million in emergency conditions, and it has been observed that food security has significantly deteriorated since the escalation began. Wheat flour prices increased by 10 per cent in parts of Ta’iz as of late September, while traders estimate wheat stocks will cover only about two months of demand. At the UN General Assembly, 80 countries supported a statement condemning “the Houthis’ decision to resume the conflict in Yemen, their continuous strikes on Saudi Arabia, and their reckless attacks on the Red Sea.” UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg met with AA negotiators in Muscat to avoid further escalation and held talks in Cairo with the regional powers, including Egypt and the League of Arab States.

item.title: Drone strikes in Sudan leave children with nowhere to escape as conflict worsens
item.description:
Country: Sudan
Source: World Vision
  • More than 800 civilians, including children, have been killed with nearly 100,000 in Blue Nile displaced
  • This month 25 strikes have been recorded in 11 states, with hospitals, power stations, markets and homes all being targeted
  • World Vision calls on all sides to stop killing children and let essential aid flow

Drone strikes are killing hundreds of people in Sudan every month, leaving children and families facing hunger, a lack of clean water, and increased security risks as the number of drone strikes continues to escalate, says World Vision, which is calling on all sides to stop targeting civilians.

At least 880 civilians have been killed between January and May 2026, accounting for approximately 80 per cent of all civilian deaths. Civilians are being killed in markets, hospitals, displacement camps, and transport hubs.

TJ Grant, National Director, World Vision New Zealand, says, "Children and civilians are not collateral damage. Even if they aren’t targeted directly, they are the ones that suffer the consequences when essential services are targeted."

"Without power clean water cannot be pumped, hospitals can’t function, and health centres can’t keep medicines and vaccines safe. Parents risk their lives every time they go to the market to buy food. Aid agencies are also facing tough choices, often forced to cancel aid trips due to drone activity, leaving thousands without the vital support they desperately need."

Last month alone, more than 300 people in Sudan were killed, most of them civilians.

At least 25 strikes have been recorded across 11 states so far this month, including areas far from active frontlines. In Damazin, the Blue Nile State capital, drone strikes hit the Rosieres Dam Transmission Station and the city’s power plant, cutting electricity.

The situation is worsening, according to the latest figures from the Sudan INGO Forum, of which World Vision is a member. Attacks on infrastructure are impacting power supplies, health care provisions, and people’s ability to buy food and fuel. In one day alone, drones struck six power stations, disrupting electricity across south-east Sudan.

Simon Mane, National Director for World Vision Sudan, says: "This must stop. Children and civilians have already fled fighting. Now the drones are following them, leaving them with no place to run."

Mass casualty incidents are also increasing. A 26 October attack on a market in Nyala, South Darfur, killed or injured more than 150 people, while a drone strike near Amiet Market and Todach in the Abyei area on 19 October left dozens more civilians dead or injured.

Mane says, "Drones are targeting the power, fuel, and water supplies people depend on to survive. When a power station is hit, the consequences reach far beyond the site itself, affecting a child on oxygen in hospital, a patient needing dialysis, and families are left without access to clean water."

Security conditions in Blue Nile continue to deteriorate, with nearly 100,000 people displaced and growing fears of hunger as El Niño threatens the critical harvest season.

World Vision Sudan staff are providing life-saving assistance to hundreds of thousands of children and families on both sides of the conflict. However, movement restrictions, fuel shortages, and rising costs are making it difficult to reach those in need.

World Vision calls for all sides to:

  • Stop targeting civilians and essential infrastructure (power, fuel and water systems)
  • Protect displacement sites from fighting
  • Permit humanitarian access and support for displaced and host communities affected by ongoing violence
  • Allow civilians to access farms, grazing lands, and agricultural and market infrastructure during this critical harvest period to prevent widespread hunger

-ENDS-

For more information contact:

Ashley Miln | Media and PR Advisor, World Vision

item.title: World: MSF calls for stronger AMR response to protect people affected by conflict
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Rome, 18 Nov 26 - As the world marks World Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Awareness Week, MSF called on governments and funders to recognize the enormous toll that antimicrobial resistance is taking in conflict-affected and humanitarian contexts and act urgently by better equipping communities to prevent, detect, and respond to drug-resistant infections - before, during, and after times of acute crisis. Over two billion people are estimated to live in conflict-affected settings, and, in 2025, forced displacement affected an unprecedented 122 million people.

In specific, at the Fourth Plenary Assembly of the AMR Multi-Stakeholder Partnership Platform held in Rome, Italy this week, MSF asked governments and funders to:

• Invest before crises to fund national AMR plans that strengthen infection prevention and control (IPC), water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), stewardship and laboratories

• Plan for crises along with affected communities to build AMR into emergency preparedness and adapt national AMR plans in protracted crises, implementing context-specific interventions

• Protect health care to uphold international humanitarian law

• Count everyone to include conflict settings in surveillance and research, and ensure equitable access to antimicrobials and diagnostics

“For the people we treat, antimicrobial resistance is not a 2050 projection. It is a newborn with sepsis, or a person with a war wound, whose infection no longer responds to the antibiotics we have,” said Dr Cecilia Ferreyra, infectious diseases specialist and Deputy to the International Medical Secretary of MSF. “The global fight against antimicrobial resistance will fail if it leaves behind people who are living through conflict and displacement. We are asking governments and donors for dedicated funding and adapted national AMR plans that include people vulnerable to crises from the start. The commitments made here and in the Ministerial Conference in Abuja next month will help decide whether these patients still have medical tools that work.”

The risks and consequences of AMR are especially acute in settings affected by conflict and humanitarian crises, where inadequate WASH measures, poor infection prevention and control, and limited access to microbiology, diagnostic capacity, and appropriate antimicrobials contribute to emergence and spread of drug-resistant infections. Destruction of healthcare facilities and infrastructure for water and sanitation, shortages of healthcare workers, disrupted supply chains, and overcrowded living conditions further compound the AMR crisis. ​

MSF addresses AMR in more than 20 countries through over 50 projects, focusing on infection prevention and control, antibiotic stewardship, microbiology-based diagnostics, and surveillance. Our teams see the diversity of ways in which crises subject people to risk for and from AMR. From treating patients with severe wounds and drug-resistant infections to caring for malnourished children and newborns with sepsis, and people living with HIV who develop opportunistic infections, MSF works to strengthen healthcare workers’ capacity to counter AMR through provision of quality, people-centered care.

“Antimicrobial resistance is increasingly becoming a consequence of conflict, displacement and fragile health systems,” said Dr Rupa Kanapathipillai, Antimicrobial Stewardship Lead, MSF Operational Centre Paris. “In Gaza, facilities designed for 250–300 patients a day received as many as 700, with wound care provided from shared trolleys. In South Sudan, Ethiopia and Nigeria, where displacement, flooding and outbreaks hit already stretched clinics, premature babies with sepsis and severely malnourished children are being treated where our antibiograms show high resistance, even in remote areas. Resistance follows displacement and weak health systems, not just the front line.”

Global initiatives, including the updated Global Action Plan on AMR (adopted in May 2026), the planned launch of the Independent Panel for Evidence for Action against AMR, at the 5th Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on AMR in Abuja, Nigeria (6–8 December 2026), offer important opportunities to accelerate action. These initiatives are particularly crucial in light of recent shocks to global health and humanitarian financing that are taking us backwards rather than ahead. ​

“At the upcoming Ministerial Conference in Nigeria, governments must make concrete commitments and ensure that the Independent Panel on Evidence for Action against AMR will close critical evidence gaps in conflict-affected and humanitarian settings and translating evidence into action,” said Pauline Londeix, Advocacy Advisor, MSF Access. “Meaningful representation of humanitarian actors, affected communities and low-income countries is also essential to guarantee the Panel’s work responds to the needs of people most at risk.”

For interviews, please contact:

Mildred Wanyonyi: +254720260618 / mildred.wanyonyi@nairobi.msf.org

item.title: In South Sudan, New Lifelines for Mothers and Babies
item.description:
Country: South Sudan
Source: Direct Relief

In a region where pregnant women still face dangerous journeys to give birth, emergency transportation and medical supplies are helping transform maternal care.

On September 21, a pregnant woman collapsed in a remote South Sudanese town, where reaching a hospital can mean hours of travel along roads that become nearly impassable in the rainy season.

But for the first time, help came on three wheels.

One of four newly launched motorcycle ambulances rushed the woman to Mother Teresa Hospital, marking a lifesaving first-day test of an emergency transport system designed to reach mothers in some of the country’s most isolated communities, including displacement camps.

South Sudan has the world’s highest estimated neonatal mortality rate, with roughly one in 25 babies dying within their first 28 days of life, according to United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation data published last year. South Sudan also has one of the world’s highest maternal mortality rates, with an estimated 692 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2023.

Against that backdrop, local health workers report a striking development.

“It has given us the good news up to now. We have no neonatal deaths and no deaths of the mother,” said Joseph Makuach, health coordinator for Transformation of the World in Christ, or TWIC, a local organization, which shares its acronym with the South Sudanese county of Twic, that coordinates medical services.

Working alongside a network of community clinics and Mother Teresa Hospital, the ambulance, which was funded by Direct Relief partner MAMA Project, transports women in labor and patients experiencing obstetric emergencies to facilities equipped to provide care. Recent shipments of midwife kits from Direct Relief have added essential supplies needed for safer deliveries.

Reaching Mothers Before It’s Too Late

TWIC, the nonprofit, supports six primary health care clinics serving rural communities and internally displaced people. The clinics are located in Ayak Makot, Biemnhom, Bombil, Akotong, Madou, and Gogrial West.

The new fleet of motorcycle ambulances, built in Uganda, helps connect these communities with Mother Teresa Hospital and other local healthcare facilities operated by international NGOs. The vehicles have proved unexpectedly effective in difficult terrain. Unlike heavier ambulances, the motorcycles can navigate narrow, damaged roads and can be pushed free when they become stuck in mud.

When a woman needs emergency transport, community members contact TWIC staff, who coordinate with drivers and the receiving hospital. The vehicles have drivers and fuel available to respond.

The Supplies Behind Safer Deliveries

Transportation, however, is only part of the challenge.

Mother Teresa Hospital, the principal referral hospital in Twic County, has long struggled with shortages of essential medical supplies and adequately compensated health workers.

Direct Relief recently provided 15 midwife kits through TWIC’s partner network, with distributions to Mother Teresa Hospital, Lighthouse Hospital in Aweil, and nursing and midwifery partners associated with Juba Teaching Hospital.

The donated supplies include sterile gauze, gloves, umbilical cord clamps, disinfectants, and medicines such as magnesium sulfate and misoprostol, used in managing complications of pregnancy and childbirth. Together, the materials help health workers maintain hygienic conditions and respond to emergencies.

Dr. Luka Matik, director of Mother Teresa Hospital, said the supplies have improved conditions for mothers and newborns during both vaginal and cesarean deliveries.

“Safety and hygiene, they ensure safety for the mothers and babies,” Matik said, explaining that clean delivery practices reduce the risk of infections.

Matik said deliveries at the hospital have increased since the kits arrived, an indication, he believes, that women are gaining confidence in the care available.

“If a mother comes and delivers and sees she’s well taken care of, she will go ahead and spread the word,” he said.

In October, the hospital performed 20 cesarean sections, including procedures for women referred from surrounding health facilities.

The impact of the donated supplies extends to Aweil, in neighboring Northern Bahr el Ghazal state. At Lighthouse Hospital and its outreach centers, health workers recorded 180 deliveries resulting in 182 newborns in October, according to a report submitted to Direct Relief. The facilities also provided antenatal care to 480 clients and referred five women to Aweil Civil Hospital for cesarean sections. No maternal deaths were recorded during the month.

For Teresa Paul, a midwife at Lighthouse Hospital, the difference is apparent when women arrive in labor, particularly at night.

“Before the kits arrived, we often struggled with shortages of gloves, plastic sheets, cord clamps and chlorhexidine,” she said in a statement included in the hospital’s report. “When a mother came into labor at night, and supplies were not available, it was heartbreaking.”

“Now we can reassure mothers that essential delivery supplies are ready.”

For some patients, the benefits are also financial. Mary Abuk Garang, a 32-year-old mother who received care at Lighthouse Hospital, said she arrived without the supplies needed for childbirth.

“I came with nothing, but I received what I needed for my delivery,” she said in a testimonial provided by the hospital.

Dr. Repent Khamis George, principal of the Juba College of Nursing and Midwives, said midwife kits were distributed to three primary health care centers around Juba, the nation’s capital, where staff welcomed supplies that are often difficult to obtain.

Progress Amid Persistent Shortages

Despite the reported improvements, formidable challenges remain.

Matik said Mother Teresa Hospital needs additional surgical nurses, disinfectants, cleaning materials, intravenous fluids, catheters, and basic linens. Some health workers have gone months without government-funded incentive payments, placing additional pressure on colleagues supported by TWIC.

Even as these personnel challenges and other stark issues remain, Makuach, TWIC’s health coordinator, assessed recent developments in lives saved.

“Our situation is not like before,” he said.

Since 2025, Direct Relief has provided $3.2 million in medical aid to support the health work of Transformation of the World in Christ in South Sudan.

item.title: Afghanistan: Humanitarian Update, October 2026
item.description:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Funding shortfalls threaten winter response in Afghanistan

As temperatures begin to fall across Afghanistan, humanitarian partners are ramping up winter preparedness amid significant funding constraints. Aid organizations are pre-positioning supplies to enable them to deliver assistance before access to remote communities becomes more challenging. With needs expected to remain high, the humanitarian response enters the winter season facing a substantial funding gap, raising concerns about being able to reach all those in need and forcing difficult choices about how the limited resources are prioritized.

The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan requires US$1.71 billion to provide life-saving assistance and protection across Afghanistan. However, as of October, only $550 million has been received through the Plan, meaning 68 per cent of funding requirements remain unmet. This shortfall threatens efforts to support vulnerable communities during one of the most challenging seasons of the year.

Winter often brings heightened humanitarian risks across Afghanistan. In many provinces, heavy snowfall and freezing temperatures can isolate communities, disrupt transportation routes and limit access to markets, health facilities and other essential services. For households already struggling with poverty, food insecurity, climate-related shocks and limited livelihood opportunities, the cold season brings additional pressure as families seek to secure food, heating fuel, warm clothing and adequate shelter.

As winter approaches, many vulnerable families are expected to face increasing pressure as food prices, heating costs and other seasonal expenses rise while livelihood opportunities decline. Yet several critical sectors remain significantly underfunded.

Food Security and Agriculture, the largest sector in the humanitarian response, has received only 18.2 per cent of its funding requirements despite continued concerns over food insecurity across the country. As winter conditions reduce income-generating opportunities and increase household expenditure on food, fuel and other essentials, many families are likely to face greater difficulties in meeting their basic needs.

Emergency Shelter and Non-Food Items cluster, which provides vulnerable households with shelter support, essential household items and winter assistance, has received only 15.1 per cent of the funding required. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene programmes are similarly underfunded, with just 16.6 per cent of requirements met, while Nutrition activities have received 16.3 per cent. Health is funded at 45.4 per cent, leaving significant gaps in essential services, particularly as winter conditions increase the risk of respiratory infections and other seasonal illnesses.

Together, these funding shortfalls risk limiting access to food, shelter, health care, safe water and nutrition support during one of the most challenging periods of the year, potentially leaving vulnerable households with fewer options to cope.

item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Nutrition Cluster, UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

La réunion conjointe PRONANUT-Cluster Nutrition du 27 octobre 2026 a réuni environ 60 partenaires. Les échanges ont porté sur la méthodologie de calcul des personnes dans le besoin pour le HNRP 2027, la préparation de la revue annuelle 2026 du PRONANUT, la réponse nutritionnelle à Ebola dans les CTE/CT et les interventions des partenaires.

Les discussions ont mis en évidence un faible niveau de rapportage et des besoins nutritionnels encore non couverts. Elles ont souligné la nécessité de renforcer la coordination, d’actualiser les projets dans Activity Info (HPC 2026) et de concentrer les interventions sur les zones prioritaires insuffisamment couvertes.

item.title: DR Congo: Cluster Protection RDC : Aperçu du monitoring de protection au Nord-Kivu - Faits saillants et tendances majeures du mois de octobre 2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Sources: Protection Cluster, UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

En octobre 2026, la situation de protection au Sud-Kivu s’est considérablement détériorée, marquée par une intensification des affrontements entre groupes armés dans les territoires de Walungu, Kabare, Kalehe, Mwenga et Fizi. Cette dégradation se serait traduite par la présence d’engins explosifs dans des zones d’habitation, des actes de représailles, ainsi que des recrutements forcés, y compris d’enfants.

●Forte hausse des violations des droits : 2 466 violations ont été identifiées en octobre, soit +62% par rapport à septembre (1 524), le niveau le plus élevé depuis juin.

●Engins explosifs : Des engins explosifs auraient été lancés lors des affrontements à Kaziba, dans le territoire de Walungu, causant la mort de plusieurs civils, dont une femme et ses deux enfants, ainsi que la destruction d’une école.

●Recrutement d’enfants : 44 allégations de recrutement et d’utilisation d’enfants ont été documentées, notamment à Kalehe, Mwenga, Fizi et dans la plaine de la Ruzizi.

●Représailles : Des civils accusés de collaboration auraient été arrêtés, torturés et auraient vu leurs maisons incendiées, notamment à Itombwe (Mwenga) et à Kabare.

item.title: oPt: Gaza's Education Crisis: A System-Wide Collapse Threatening an Entire Generation
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: American Near East Refugee Aid

Please refer to the attached file.

AN ENTIRE GENERATION OUT OF SCHOOL

The war that began on October 7, 2023 did not just interrupt schooling in Gaza, it dismantled the education system that more than 750,000 learners, from preschool through university, once relied on.1 Nearly all schools have been damaged or destroyed, and for over two years, students of all ages have had little to no access to formal learning.

A child who was seven when this began is now nine or ten, and has spent a third of the life that they can remember waiting for school to resume.

This report is based on Anera's Gaza Education Sector Needs Assessment, which draws on interviews and focus group discussions with teachers, parents, students, education officials and community members across Gaza, alongside secondary data from UNRWA, UNICEF, the Education Cluster, the Palestine Central Bureau of Statistics and other humanitarian and education partners.

What emerges is a story of systemic collapse in education, one that has stripped away not just classrooms, but the routines, relationships and sense of future that schooling once provided. The war's psychological toll is equally profound. Children have endured repeated familial displacement, loss and violence, while teachers are coping with their own trauma even as they try to support students.

Yet, despite overwhelming challenges, Gaza's communities continue to demonstrate remarkable tenacity. Parents, volunteers and educators have created informal classrooms and learning activities wherever possible, underscoring the determination to keep young people learning and the urgent need for sustained international support. Children cannot recover academically without first having stability, routine and protection. Restoring education in Gaza should therefore begin with three essentials: safe places to learn, teachers who are supported and able to teach, and basic classroom resources.

This report tells the story of what has been lost and lays out what must happen next.

item.title: 2025 Annual Report: Libya: Division Entrenches Violations and Undermines Accountability [EN/AR]
item.description:
Country: Libya
Source: Libya Crimes Watch

Please refer to the attached files.

Libya Crimes Watch Issues Its 2025 Annual Report

London, 8 April 2026 — Libya Crimes Watch (LCW) has published its 2025 Annual Report, entitled “LIBYA: DIVISION ENTRENCHES VIOLATIONS AND UNDERMINES ACCOUNTABILITY“, documenting the continued and escalating grave human rights violations and international crimes occurring across the country, against a backdrop of the absence of effective accountability pathways and the persistence of impunity.

The report records 859 grave violations documented during 2025, compared to 589 during 2024, reflecting a significant increase in the rate of violations. It draws primarily on 93 documentation files and direct testimonies from victims, survivors, and witnesses collected by LCW’s field team in accordance with LCW’s established documentation methodology, which is aligned with international protocols for the documentation of human rights violations. These violations affected 617 civilians and occurred across at least 29 major areas and cities in eastern, southern, and western Libya, including remote and hard-to-reach areas.

The report provides a legal analysis of the documented violations in light of IHRL and IHL, drawing on indicators that measure the gravity, patterns, and scale of violations, and concludes that certain of these violations may constitute international crimes by virtue of their systematic nature and scale.

The Annual Report highlights the continuation of serious patterns of violations, including arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, torture and ill-treatment, extrajudicial killing, and the denial of basic fair trial guarantees, alongside trafficking in persons, forced labour, and sexual violence. It further documents the repeated targeting of human rights defenders, activists, journalists, and dissidents for exercising their fundamental rights, including freedom of expression and participation in public life.

The report addresses violations committed against migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees, as well as vulnerable and marginalised groups, including women, children, and religious, ethnic, and gender minorities, and highlights the various contexts in which these violations occurred, including casualties resulting from military operations, encompassing armed clashes and the explosion of ERW.

The 2025 Annual Report identifies the responsibility of the authorities in eastern and western Libya for these violations, as well as that of prominent commanders and officials, whether for their commission by affiliated or supporting security apparatuses and armed groups, or for their failure to fulfil legal obligations to prevent violations, protect civilians, investigate incidents, and ensure the accountability of perpetrators. The report further highlights the continued inability of the national justice system to conduct independent and effective investigations, and the persistent weakness of cooperation with international justice mechanisms, including the ICC.

Commenting on the report, Ali Omar, Executive Director of Libya Crimes Watch, stated:

“Every year we find ourselves confronted with the same patterns of violations recurring, whilst victims and their families continue to await justice. This reality reflects an ongoing failure by the Libyan authorities to halt violations and hold those responsible to account, and underscores the urgent need for serious action to bring an end to impunity.”

In its recommendations, LCW affirms the urgent need to take concrete steps to end grave violations and international crimes, ensure the accountability of those responsible, and end impunity, including through full cooperation with the ICC. It calls upon the authorities in eastern and western Libya to honour their legal obligations, guarantee the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, and cease the targeting of civilians on account of their opinions or activities. It further urges the international community to support justice and accountability pathways and to cease any direct or indirect support to parties implicated in violations.

Description

The report, “The Cost of EU-Libya Cooperation on Migration: Serious Human Rights Violations against Migrants, Refugees and Asylum Seekers,” is a joint analytical report by the International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) and Libya Crimes Watch (LCW).It documents patterns of serious human rights violations against migrants in Libya and provides a multidimensional analysis of the role of European migration management policies in perpetuating and exacerbating these violations. The report also presents a set of recommendations addressed to Libya, the European Union and its Member States, focusing on ending violations against migrants in Libya and ensuring the protection of their rights.

item.title: Haiti: Rapport de situation octobre 2026
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

La situation humanitaire en Haïti est demeurée marquée par des déplacements massifs et des préoccupations persistantes en matière de protection en octobre 2026. De nouveaux épisodes de violence armée ont continué de provoquer d’importants mouvements de population, particulièrement dans le département de l’Artibonite, où les violences ont déplacé plus de 13,900 personnes selon la DTM de l’OIM. La majorité des personnes touchées ont trouvé refuge auprès de familles d’accueil, tandis que d’autres se sont installées dans des sites de déplacement. Cette extension géographique de la violence au-delà de Port-au-Prince vers les zones rurales et périphériques contribue à l’augmentation des pressions liées aux déplacements et à l’aggravation des besoins humanitaires dans les départements touchés. Bien que les besoins multisectoriels persistants aient continué de dépasser les capacités disponibles dans de nombreuses localités, l’OIM et ses partenaires ont poursuivi la fourniture d’une assistance vitale, notamment dans les domaines de l’abri, de l’eau, de l’assainissement et de l’hygiène (EAH), de la santé, de la protection et de la gestion des sites, tout en faisant progresser les efforts de relèvement et de stabilisation là où les conditions le permettaient.

item.title: Haiti: Hait Situation Report October 2026
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

Haiti’s humanitarian situation remained marked by largescale displacement and persistent protection concerns in October 2026. New incidents of armed violence continued to trigger significant population movements, particularly in Artibonite Department, where violence displaced more than 13,900 people according to IOM DTM. The majority of individuals sought refuge with host families, while others relocated to displacement sites. This geographic spread of violence beyond Port-au-Prince into rural and peripheral areas is contributing to growing displacement pressures and deepening humanitarian needs across affected departments. Although sustained multisectoral needs outpaced available capacities in many locations, IOM and partners continued to deliver life-saving assistance, including shelter, WASH, health, protection and site management support, while advancing recovery and stabilization efforts where conditions permitted.

item.title: At least 64 children killed and 64 injured in Yemen as intensified hostilities approach three-month mark
item.description:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Children's Fund

NEW YORK, 18 November 2026 – At least 64 children have been killed and 64 injured in Yemen since hostilities escalated on 3 September. The number of casualties is likely to increase as renewed fighting continues around densely populated areas, particularly in Taiz and Lahj.

“The rising number of children killed and injured in Yemen is devastating. It must stop,” said UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russell. “Behind every number is a child whose life has been cut short or changed forever.”

Basic services and infrastructure children depend on are also being directly impacted. At least seven schools and 28 health facilities, including five supported by UNICEF, have been damaged since the escalation began. On 2 November, an attack on the UNICEF-supported Al-Suqyah Health Centre in Lahj, which serves around 1,700 people, was reported to have killed five people, including three health workers.

At the same time, displacement is accelerating. More than 330,000 people, including an estimated 174,000 children, have been displaced since the beginning of the renewed military escalations. Many displaced families are sheltering in unfinished or damaged buildings and struggling to access food, safe water, and health care.

The situation in Taiz City is particularly alarming. With the main road from Aden closed and alternative routes insecure, more than 800,000 people have reportedly been cut off from humanitarian assistance as of late October. Water production has fallen by nearly 50 per cent, food and fuel prices have more than doubled, and shortages of medicines, fuel, medical oxygen and electricity are threatening emergency, maternal, and newborn care.

Across escalation-impacted areas, over 1,160 schools have closed or suspended learning, affecting more than half a million students. Meanwhile, around one in three children recently screened by UNICEF mobile health teams were found to be acutely malnourished. Overcrowded displacement sites, too few latrines, and limited access to safe water are also increasing the risk of disease.

UNICEF is expanding its emergency response to reach up to 350,000 people, redeploying health and nutrition mobile teams to displacement sites and affected communities in Aden, Lahj, Abyan, Marib and Taiz, scaling up emergency water and sanitation support, and providing psychosocial care and case management for children, including those who are unaccompanied or separated from their families.

“Yemen’s children have suffered so much. We urgently need safe and unimpeded humanitarian access,” said Russell. “All parties must comply with their obligations under international law. Children must be protected, including their access to essential services such as healthcare, education, safe water, and food.”

item.title: World: Community-led negotiations
item.description:
Country: World
Source: Centre of Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation

Please refer to the attached file.

The Centre for Competence on Humanitarian Negotiation (CCHN) commissioned the Humanitarian Policy Group at ODI Global to conduct research on community-led negotiations, particularly the processes that community negotiators undertake to engage with authorities and armed actors for
humanitarian access and protection.

Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following research questions:

  • What triggers the decision to engage in direct negotiations?
  • How do community negotiators prepare for such engagements?
  • What is the process taken in negotiations?
  • What are their risk-mitigation strategies?
  • What are the tactics and strategies used in the negotiation process?
  • What factors influence the outcome of negotiations?
  • What follow-up actions take place once an agreement is reached?
  • What type of support do community negotiators most need?

The findings presented in this report identified that community negotiation practices are often instinctual, unstructured, and rarely documented. Stemming from 13 countries across diverse contexts, the results strongly suggest that community negotiators prepare strategically for dialogue, similarly to what is set out in the Naivasha Grid. As noted, the greater the international support, the more aligned the community negotiations become with international humanitarian practices. However, the process varies according to the context and is generally more organic than international negotiation practices.
